attempts.raw_response: This biological advantage allows breeds like Huskies or Malamutes to withstand freezing conditions with ease, whereas short-haired or small breeds may struggle significantly. However, even cold-adapted dogs require protection during extreme weather events. Always monitor your pet for signs of discomfort, such as lifting paws or shivering, which indicate that the temperature has become too harsh. Applying protective balms can prevent ice buildup between toes and keep pads moisturized against cracking. Remember that individual tolerance varies widely; a healthy young dog might enjoy a brisk winter walk, while an older companion needs shorter, warmer outings. Prioritize safety by checking local weather advisories and limiting exposure time when temperatures drop below freezing.

pair.human_continuation: Once you have brought your dog in from the cold, be sure to remove any ice, snow, or water that has accumulated on its paws. This will help keep the paws healthy and will minimize the chance of frostbite or raw skin.  Be sure to check between the toes for ice and snow. Sometimes ice balls can form between a dog's toes. If you notice your dog limping during the walk, make sure there aren't ice balls stuck to its paws. Wiping down the paws can also remove some of the salt and chemicals that can accumulate on the surface of pads. One of the major hazards for your dog's paws in winter is the salt or chemicals that are used to deice roads and sidewalks.
pair.prefix: A young, healthy dog is also more likely to thrive in cold weather than a very old dog. Take your dog's physical condition into consideration when taking it out in cold weather. The paws of dogs bred to live in cold temperatures are different from other dog paws. The blood in their paws is rewarmed faster and the pads themselves are made of more cold-resistant tissue.
